sections.html:
Three roles split the work in Williamson County. Elected commissioners and city boards set the rates, the Property Assessor appraises, and the Trustee turns both into bills and collects the money. The Trustee's office is in Suite 203 at 1320 West Main Street in Franklin (zip 37064). Call 615-790-5709 or stop by on weekdays between 8:00 and 4:30. Questions about your value or a change of address go to the Assessor at 615-790-5708.

The Trustee bills for Williamson County itself, the Franklin Special School District, Brentwood, Franklin, Nolensville and Thompson's Station. Owners in Spring Hill and Fairview should phone their city hall to find out which office handles the city portion of the bill.

The Trustee cannot forgive anything. Under T.C.A. 67-5-2803 the office has no power to waive, prorate or release any part of the tax or its interest, so a late bill stays late.

Williamson County is a high-value Middle Tennessee market. It counted 272,061 people as of July 2025, up 9.8% from the April 2020 base, and has 103,674 housing units, with 78.8% of occupied homes lived in by their owners. A typical owned home is worth $751,900, and 1,621 building permits were issued in 2025. Brentwood and Franklin anchor the north end, while the south keeps more of its farm character. Williamson County Schools covers most of the county, and part of Franklin sends kindergarten through eighth graders to the Franklin Special School District.

The state sets the assessment ratios: 25 percent of appraised value for a home, 40 percent for commercial and industrial property, and 30 percent for business personal property. The rate is then applied to each $100 of the assessed figure. A higher appraisal therefore feeds straight into a higher bill.

The county posts its 2026 rates as a chart on its Property Tax Rates page. The county rate is combined with whichever city or school district applies to the address. The Assessor values new construction up to September 1, and then the rolls pass to the Trustee.

The roll opens to the public in May, and owners whose value changed get a notice by mail. Look at it early, because that leaves time to act before the June hearing window.

Bills go out in early October. From the first Monday that month through the last day of February, you can pay with no added charge, including in installments. Starting March 1, the Trustee adds 1.5 percent, and adds it again at the start of every following month. One bill covers a single calendar year.

If your lender pays from escrow, you still receive a statement, which the Trustee describes as a copy for your records. Ask the Trustee's office which payment methods it takes for the 2026 bill.

Payment windowDatesAdded charge
Interest-free periodFirst Monday in October through the end of FebruaryNone
Late periodMarch 1 onward1.5 percent, added at the start of each month

Two rules matter once a sale is on the table. The bill follows the owner of record on January 1, so a seller who has sold since then should hand it to the buyer. And nobody at the counter can erase interest.

Start by calling the Assessor at 615-790-5708 and asking how the value was reached. Many disputes end right there. Even so, you need to book a hearing slot with the county equalization board to keep your appeal rights intact. Five residents sit on that board, each named by the County Commission to a two-year term. It hears cases in June, and the Assessor's staff ask owners to phone during the first week of June. Only the person on the roll, an authorized agent or the owner can file.

The next stop after a county hearing is the State Board of Equalization. It accepts filings until August 1 of the tax year, or until 45 days after the county notice if that date is later, and its administrative judge issues a decision within 90 days of the hearing. Sales of comparable properties are the best proof for a house, and an unsupported claim of overvaluation rarely works. Pay the undisputed part of the tax before March 1 so no interest builds while the appeal runs.

The Trustee administers four programs, two of them state-funded, and appointments are required. Disabled veterans and their widows or widowers have a separate state program, so call for the paperwork it needs. Each program counts 2025 income from every source for the applicant, spouse and co-owners, and the elderly programs require the applicant to reach 65 by the end of 2026. Income limits for tax year 2026:

ProgramCombined 2025 income limit
State relief, elderly or disabled$38,470
County Broad Base relief, elderly$63,000
County Tax Freeze, age 65 or older$69,150

Applications for 2026 relief are taken after the 2026 bill arrives and until April 5, 2027, and the tax must be paid in full first. The freeze fixes the home's tax at the qualifying year's amount for as long as the owner re-qualifies every year. It covers the residence and up to 5 acres, and the base resets if improvements raise the value or the owner buys another home. Call 615-790-5709 to book.

The January 1 owner receives the statement. A seller who closes in the fall still gets the 2026 mailing and has to pass it along to the buyer. Ask the title company how the year will be divided on the settlement statement.

A short routine keeps things clean. Call the Trustee at 615-790-5709 before you sign a contract and ask for the balance on your parcel. Give that figure to the closing agent so the county can be paid from your proceeds in one step. If you are enrolled in the freeze, talk to the Trustee first, because selling and then buying another home resets the base amount.

Taxes that are already past due carry interest every month from March 1, and the Trustee cannot reduce it. A buyer's lender will want the bill current, so unpaid tax is best settled before closing rather than after. A cash buyer can skip the lender's review of tax status, but the county's balance still has to be cleared at the table.

faqs.q: Where is the Williamson County Trustee's office?
faqs.a: Go to Suite 203 at 1320 West Main Street in Franklin. The office is staffed weekdays from 8:00 to 4:30, and the number is 615-790-5709.

faqs.q: What is the last day to pay without interest?
faqs.a: February 28 is the last interest-free day. The 1.5 percent monthly charge begins March 1.

faqs.q: Can the Trustee forgive interest on a late bill?
faqs.a: No. State law leaves the Trustee without authority to waive, prorate or release any of the tax or its interest.

faqs.q: How much income can a household have and still qualify for the tax freeze?
faqs.a: The limit for tax year 2026 is $69,150 of combined 2025 income across the applicant, spouse and co-owners. The applicant must also turn 65 by December 31, 2026.

faqs.q: Who do I call about an appraisal?
faqs.a: The Property Assessor's line is 615-790-5708. To reach the county equalization board, call that office during the first week of June.
